sentences.text: Arrhinoceratops is a genus of herbivorous ceratopsian dinosaur whose name means "no nose-horn face".
The only known species, Arrhinoceratops brachyops, lived in North America about 70 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Maastrichtian.
Its snout is short and high, while the sides of the neck frill are adorned by approximately nine osteoderms and the rear edge is slightly scalloped.
W. A. Parks described the genus in 1925 based on a partially crushed skull that lacked lower jaws.
The remains were collected in 1923 from the Neill's Ranch site along the Red Deer River in Alberta by a University of Toronto expedition.
The holotype specimen ROM 796 was found in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation dating to the latest Campanian or earliest Maastrichtian.
Material found in Utah in the 1930s was named Arrhinoceratops? utahensis by Charles Whitney Gilmore in 1946, though Gilmore himself doubted the identification.
Douglas A. Lawson transferred the Utah species to the genus Torosaurus in 1976, renaming it Torosaurus utahensis.
Arrhinoceratops lived in a wet coastal environment with warm summers and cool winters that was densely forested.
Because flowering plants were geographically limited during the Cretaceous, Arrhinoceratops likely fed on ferns, cycads, and conifers.
Arrhinoceratops was likely preyed upon by the dinosaur Albertosaurus.
A pathological opening on the left squamosal of the holotype suggests the animal may have suffered a wound.
Modern research classifies Arrhinoceratops as a member of the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
Cladistic analyses place Arrhinoceratops close to Anchiceratops.
Arrhinoceratops is closely related to the genera Torosaurus, Chasmosaurus, and Pentaceratops.
The dinosaur belongs to the family Ceratopsidae and is classified within the class Ornithischia.
Arrhinoceratops lived during the latest Campanian or earliest Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 83.6 to 66 million years ago.
Helen Tyson concluded that Arrhinoceratops was closely related to Torosaurus and possibly its direct ancestor.
Richard Swann Lull was critical of Parks' original description in 1933, and later research by Helen Tyson confirmed that Parks made many mistakes.
